# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### High VolumeQueueLength on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** Alarm example-d-gp3-queue-length went into ALARM at 16:51:48 UTC. Average VolumeQueueLength was 15.998 at 16:48, 16:49 and 16:50 UTC, against a threshold of 4. The volume is a 20 GiB gp3 (3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s) in us-east-1a, account 012345678901_1, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_2 at /dev/sdf.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:48:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: Running FIS experiment injects an I/O fault on the volume
**Description:** FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (template EXT1234567890abcdef_4, 'example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency', role example-fis) was started by example-session at 16:47:04Z. Its aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action has been running on vol-0123456789abcdef0 since 16:47:16Z. It adds 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads for PT60M, so it should end around 17:47Z. The template was last edited at 16:47:01Z and has no stop conditions.
**Cascades to:** cause-queue-saturation, symptom-ebs-d-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 is running:** Experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 uses template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 and role example-fis. It started at 16:47:04 UTC and targets only vol-0123456789abcdef0. Its action aws:ebs:volume-io-latency started at 16:47:16 UTC with these parameters: 500 ms latency on 100% of writes and 50% of reads, for PT60M. The experiment has no stop conditions and is still running.

### Cause: Fixed ~16 in-flight I/Os pile up under the injected delay
**Description:** About 42 ops/s with an average wait of about 0.38 s works out to about 16 requests in flight, so the application appears to hold a fixed concurrency of about 16. With every I/O delayed, the queue saturates at about 16 and throughput falls from about 1000 IOPS to about 42 IOPS.
**Cascades to:** symptom-ebs-d-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **Write ops collapsed and the queue saturated at 16:48:** From 16:25 to 16:46 UTC the volume was steady: about 30,000 write ops and 30,000 read ops per minute (about 500 IOPS each), a queue length of about 0.77, and about 31 s of idle time per minute. From 16:48 onward, write ops were about 1,250 per minute (about 21 IOPS), total write time rose from about 28.6 s to about 640 s per minute, idle time was about 0 and the queue length was 16.0. The EC2 metrics InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0 throughout. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck and VolumeAvgWriteLatency returned no datapoints.
- **Read I/O shows the same latency pattern:** VolumeTotalReadTime rose from about 17.5 s to 316–347 s per minute from 16:48 UTC. Over the same period, VolumeReadBytes fell from about 491 MB to about 21 MB per minute. Reads are slowed along with writes, which fits latency added to each I/O.

#### Gaps
- **Application logs and metrics not inspected:** Impact on the application is inferred only from EBS latency metrics on vol-0123456789abcdef0. Application-side telemetry on i-1234567890abcdef0_2 was not reviewed.

### Hypothesis: Volume or instance IOPS/throughput limit reached
**Description:** The volume is provisioned for 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, and before the test it ran at about 1000 IOPS and about 16 MB/s. InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck read 0 throughout. IOPS fell after the test started instead of rising.
**Cascades to:** symptom-ebs-d-queue-length

#### Gaps
- **Volume-level exceeded checks returned no data:** VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck for vol-0123456789abcdef0 returned no datapoints. The conclusion that the volume is not IOPS-limited rests on comparing provisioned with actual IOPS, plus the instance-level checks.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Stop FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (with owner approval) to end the injected EBS latency; do not resize the volume

## Reasoning
The latency is injected deliberately by FIS, and the volume runs far below its 3000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s. Adding IOPS cannot remove a fixed per-I/O delay. If the owner wants the full test run, the experiment ends on its own around 17:47Z.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Pre Validate

#### 1.1 Get owner approval before ending a deliberate test
**Type:** text
Ask example-session whether stopping the example scenario d run early is acceptable. If they want the full 60 minutes, skip the apply step; the latency clears around 17:47Z.
**Purpose:** Get owner approval before ending a deliberate test

#### 1.2 Make sure the experiment is still running
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query 'experiment.state.status'
```
**Purpose:** Make sure the experiment is still running
**Advisory:** Continue only if the result is running; if it is completed or stopped there is nothing to do.

### Step 2: Apply

#### 2.1 End the latency injection so the volume returns to its pre-16:47Z…
**Type:** command
```
aws fis stop-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** End the latency injection so the volume returns to its pre-16:47Z behavior
**Risks:** Ends the eval run early, so the test results will be incomplete
**Advisory:** Only the fault injection stops; the volume, its data and the instance are not touched.

### Step 3: Post Validate

#### 3.1 Confirm the experiment and its action are stopped
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query 'experiment.[state.status,actions.latency.state.status]'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the experiment and its action are stopped

#### 3.2 Confirm the queue length falls back to about 0.77
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average --period 60 --start-time <now-15m> --end-time <now>
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the queue length falls back to about 0.77
**Advisory:** Write latency should return to about 1 ms and ops to about 30,000/min each for reads and writes.

#### 3.3 Confirm the alarm returns to OK
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-d-gp3-queue-length --region us-east-1 --query 'MetricAlarms[0].StateValue'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the alarm returns to OK
**Advisory:** Expect OK within about 3 to 5 minutes; the alarm needs 3 datapoints of 60 s before it changes state.

### Step 4: Rollback

#### 4.1 Restart the eval scenario
**Type:** command
```
aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --tags Project=example --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Restart the eval scenario
**Risks:** Injects 500 ms latency on the volume again for 60 minutes

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Add a stop condition to FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_4
**Description:** First back up the template (aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 > EXT1234567890abcdef_4-backup.json). Then add a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition, e.g. aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]. To undo, set --stop-conditions source=none. The queue-length alarm would halt this scenario about 5 minutes after it starts; for a sustained-latency test, use a dedicated guardrail alarm instead. If the template is managed as IaC, make the change in that source; where it is defined is unknown.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The template shows a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition
- A test run stops itself when that alarm fires
- The change is reflected in the IaC source, if one exists
